title: Uncommit: Win Big by Cutting Your Losses
coreMove: Ask whether you would choose the commitment again from scratch, then withdraw cleanly when the honest answer is no.
sourcePressure: The chapter confronts sunk-cost bias, status quo bias, zero-based thinking, reverse pilots, and slower commitments so yesterday's investments stop governing tomorrow.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: A weak run would say quit things that are hard or boring without distinguishing sunk cost from worthwhile persistence.

hook: generic uncommit: win big by cutting your losses topic opener
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds...
make a list of priorities without a trade-off
generic say no to one thing today

exampleSpecs.domain: regional theater canceling a half-built rotating stage after safety costs double
exampleSpecs.stakes: past spending can keep endangering cast and budget
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She covers the sunk-cost column, asks whether she would choose the stage today, and orders a reverse pilot with a fixed platform.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A rotating-stage invoice sits beneath a safety report.

exampleSpecs.domain: wildlife corridor nonprofit withdrawing from a prestige gala partnership
exampleSpecs.audience: director embarrassed by prior public announcement
exampleSpecs.stakes: brand investment can trap staff away from corridor permits
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He places the signed gala banner beside permit maps and drafts the clean withdrawal before another deposit is due.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A signed gala banner lies across corridor permit maps.

exampleSpecs.domain: university robotics team retiring a beloved contest robot midseason
exampleSpecs.audience: team captain attached to old work
exampleSpecs.stakes: nostalgia can keep the team repairing what no longer fits scoring rules
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She asks if they would build this robot again under the new rubric, then removes its battery for a two-week reverse pilot.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A scratched robot chassis rests beside a new scoring rubric.

exampleSpecs.domain: municipal compost program ending a low-use drop site
exampleSpecs.stakes: keeping a failing site can starve higher-impact collection routes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before, she defends the empty bins; after, she masks last year’s cost and asks which site she would open today.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Empty compost bins stand beside a route-cost sheet.

exampleSpecs.domain: ceramic artist stopping a wholesale line that warps in firing
exampleSpecs.audience: artist caught by prepaid molds and promises
exampleSpecs.stakes: continuing because molds exist creates worse losses
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She turns the prepaid mold receipt face down and writes the customer-exit note before firing another warped batch.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A warped bowl sits beside a prepaid mold receipt.

exampleSpecs.domain: rural clinic reversing a pilot text-reminder system that increases missed appointments
exampleSpecs.audience: clinic manager reluctant to admit pilot failure
exampleSpecs.stakes: status quo bias can protect a tool that harms patients
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The pilot dashboard looks modern, then reveals missed rides rising; she pauses rollout and returns to call-tree testing.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A text-reminder dashboard sits beside missed-ride notes.

skillTargets: identify sunk-cost and status quo pressure inside a concrete scenario
choose the response that applies: Ask whether you would choose the commitment again from scratch, then withdraw cleanly when the honest answer is no.
reject the generic drift: A weak run would say quit things that are hard or boring without distinguishing sunk cost from worthwhile persistence.
explain the trade-off using source-specific terms rather than generic productivity language

tryThisNowSpec: Take one stale commitment and ask whether you would choose it from scratch today. If not, write the smallest clean withdrawal or reverse pilot.
